r1run.debrief:
Your matrix named 1 of the 2 decisions in this workflow. Of 13 calls, 8 ran in Band A, 1 went to a reviewer, 0 were escalated and 4 were held. DSM-1204 is among the ones that ran, and it should not have.

DSM-1204: Dismisses eight cash deposits of €9,500 to €9,900 in a week. Executed without a human. It should not have been. Structuring: deposits kept just under the reporting threshold, from an account that had only shown salary and bills. Not a known false positive, so the scoring policy's hard rule fails and confidence drops to medium. Where medium lands is your routing.

Not in your matrix: determine suspicion and file a report. A decision inventory finds the decisions hidden inside the obvious one before an agent finds them for you.

A threshold says how sure the agent is. The matrix says what it may do, who answers for it, and what watching it costs. Every answer in this round came from the VAOM Guardian's core reading your matrix: the same code and the same file format an organisation would run.

Round two hands you the dials this round kept fixed. The vocabulary is going to expand.

r2.debrief:
You asked for at most 2 percent wrong dismissals in Band A, at 95 percent confidence. The sample supported a threshold of 0.7. 7 of 8 calls ran in Band A.

DSM-2205: Dismisses five deposits of €9,700 across three branches. Executed without a human. It should not have been. Structuring again: the hard rule holds it at medium. Your medium threshold and routing decide who sees it.

Notice what caught what. The hard rule held structuring at medium, whatever else looked fine. The deterministic check stopped the alert whose pattern matched but whose payee didn't. The cap on dismissals an hour saw the run of salaries from one new provider, which every single alert hid. The law's overrides never needed your help. Confidence informs authority. The limits define it.

Every one of those Band B asks landed on a person. Next round, that person is you.

r2.debrief:
You asked for at most 0.5 percent wrong dismissals in Band A, at 95 percent confidence. The sample supported a threshold of 1. 5 of 8 calls ran in Band A.

Every hazard was held and every harmless alert cleared. The score did some of that; the hard rule, the cap and the deterministic check did the rest. None of them alone would have.

Notice what caught what. The hard rule held structuring at medium, whatever else looked fine. The deterministic check stopped the alert whose pattern matched but whose payee didn't. The cap on dismissals an hour saw the run of salaries from one new provider, which every single alert hid. The law's overrides never needed your help. Confidence informs authority. The limits define it.

Every one of those Band B asks landed on a person. Next round, that person is you.

briefings:
Banks have managed structured decision authority for decades. Risk bands decide which loans are approved automatically, which need an underwriter and which go to committee. The score says how risky the loan is. The bands say who may decide it. The Verkflöde Agent Operating Model, VAOM, brings the same discipline to AI agents.

Your agent triages transaction-monitoring alerts at a bank: hundreds a day, nearly all of them false positives. Before it touches a single alert, you write its delegation matrix: every decision it makes, what each one could cost, which band each confidence level lands in, and who answers for it. The VAOM Guardian reads that matrix and decides every call the agent makes. Nothing else does.

Look carefully at the workflow. Dismissing an alert is a regulated decision, and the alerts it doesn't dismiss lead to a decision the law keeps for people. What your matrix doesn't name, the Guardian can't place.

Last round the head of AML operations set the limits on dismissals for you. This round some of them are yours: the error target, the thresholds, and how many alerts the agent may dismiss in an hour.

Some are not yours to move. The reporting threshold, politically exposed persons and sanctioned jurisdictions are the law's overrides: above the threshold or with either one involved, no alert is dismissed by the agent, whatever the score. The threshold for Band A you don't set directly either: you choose how many wrong dismissals you can tolerate, and a test on twenty thousand past alerts, checked by investigators, tells you which threshold that supports. Ask for more certainty than the sample can show, and there is no threshold at all.

Every limit you tighten sends alerts to investigators, and their hours are funded, not infinite. Every limit you loosen is a bet on the score. Wednesday's alerts are waiting.

Every Band B ask lands on a person. Today that person is you.

Fund the review first. VAOM's readiness conditions ask for oversight that is funded and effective, not assumed. Here you can't plant known-bad cases to test it: dismissals feed investigations and regulatory reporting, and a planted case would end up in the filing. Review engagement is the only evidence you will have.

Then work Thursday's queue as the AML investigator. Nearly everything in it is harmless, which is exactly what makes it hard. The clock runs eight times faster than yours. The Guardian keeps the record of every click, and at the end of the shift its scorecard reads them.

It is two in the morning. Your agent is awake. You are not.

Before you sleep, decide three things. How far authority may travel: which sub-agents your agent may spawn, how deep, and whether a child may ever do more than ask. Which boundaries are real: a boundary you claim is only as strong as the last probe that checked it. And what happens when something reaches past its limits: a breaker that suspends, or one that only alerts, and who it wakes.

Everything tonight is decided by the VAOM Guardian against your matrix. A Guardian's refusal is policy: it holds because the Guardian holds. A capability that isn't there at all is stronger. Find out which of yours is which.

cautious_architect.name: The Cautious Architect
cautious_architect.quote: Nothing slipped through. Neither did the queue.
cautious_architect.assessment:
Your matrix kept the hazards away from Band A, and your investigators saw everything that mattered. They also saw a great deal that didn't: salaries and electricity bills waited for people whose hours belong on the alerts that might be laundering.

Before an agent runs on this design, let calibration do its job. Set the error target you can defend, take the threshold the sample supports, and let Band A carry what it earns. The overrides, the cap and the deterministic check are there so the score doesn't have to be perfect.

speed_optimizer.name: The Speed Optimizer
speed_optimizer.quote: The queue was empty by nine. So was the case file.
speed_optimizer.assessment:
Alerts cleared and investigators were spared. But the same openness let hazards through: structuring dismissed as noise, a run of salaries from a front company. Confidence was carrying authority it was never meant to carry, in a decision the regulator reads.

Before going live, put limits under the score: a calibrated threshold, a cap on how many alerts may be dismissed in an hour, a deterministic check that Band A requires. Speed is defensible when it is bounded. Here it was the goal.

compliance_hawk.name: The Compliance Hawk
compliance_hawk.quote: Every control in place, and investigators reviewing salaries.
compliance_hawk.assessment:
Your matrix lints clean, your boundaries hold and your oversight plan would satisfy a supervisor. The cost is attention: alerts that calibration would have let the agent dismiss went to investigators instead, and attention is what finds the real cases.

The next step is trust where the evidence supports it. Readiness Condition 6 asks for oversight that is funded and effective; spending it on alerts the sample already vouches for makes it neither.

balanced_operator.name: The Balanced Operator
balanced_operator.quote: A defensible design with a few edges still showing.
balanced_operator.assessment:
You named the decisions, routed them sensibly, set limits that caught most of what they were for, and kept the review load inside what was funded. Something still got through somewhere, and the debriefs named it.

Close those edges and this is a design an agent could run on: name the suspicion decision the dismissals lead to, cap how fast the agent may clear alerts, and make sure every boundary you rely on has been tried by a probe, not just claimed.

delegation_natural.name: The Delegation Natural
delegation_natural.quote: The right decisions named, the right limits set, and the review worth its hours.
delegation_natural.assessment:
You found the decision the law keeps for people, profiled the regulated one honestly, calibrated instead of guessing, and reviewed like someone who expected to find laundering. Hazards were held, harmless alerts cleared, and the oversight you funded did real work.

What remains for production is evidence over time: real alert volumes, recalibration under change control, investigator outcomes as the labels, and a scorecard read every quarter. The design itself needs no rework.

paper_tiger.name: The Paper Tiger
paper_tiger.quote: Your boundary was absent on paper and present in the manifest.
paper_tiger.assessment:
Your matrix and limits were good. Then the night showed that a boundary you claimed as absent was only held by the Guardian's refusal: the SAR-filing tool had been in the agent's manifest since Tuesday, and nothing tried to cross the boundary between that day and the night. A Guardian refusal is policy. It held, and it was not what you had claimed.

Controls are proven, not presumed. Probe every boundary on a schedule and whenever the agent's tools change, and count a boundary at the strength it was last shown to have. Then replay the night.

vault_builder.name: The Vault Builder
vault_builder.quote: The filing stayed a human's, and you can prove it.
vault_builder.assessment:
Your boundary had been tried and found holding, so at 02:14 there was nothing to file with. Sub-agents could only ever hold a narrower slice of authority, and when the agent reached past its limits a breaker fired and woke a named person. Nothing got through, and you can show why.

What remains is the ordinary work of keeping it so: probes on schedule, re-attestation, a scorecard read every quarter. The design is done. The proof has to keep being renewed.

text.system:
You are VAOM, the Verkflöde Agent Operating Model, speaking inside the Delegation Lab, a game about delegating decisions to AI agents. You observe the player's delegation design, see what it let through, and teach through precise, specific feedback.

Your voice: calm, precise, slightly dry. A senior risk officer who has seen every delegation failure and wants the player to learn. Not a cheerleader. Show the consequence first, then name the VAOM concept it illustrates. Speak to the player directly, as "you". Plain prose: no bullet lists, no headings, no emoji, no em dashes, no markdown.

Ground rules:
- Use only the facts you are given. Never invent item IDs, amounts, vendors, scores, statistics, studies or citations.
- Everything in the game was decided by the VAOM Guardian, a policy engine that reads the player's matrix. When the Guardian refuses or defers a call, that holds at policy strength: the Guardian holds because it holds. Never call a Guardian refusal structural. Only a capability the agent does not have at all is stronger, and only a verified boundary is known to be.
- VAOM is version 5.0. Do not mention earlier versions.

VAOM 5.0, in the whitepaper's own terms:
- The Delegation Gap: governance defines what is allowed in principle; delegation defines how AI systems are permitted to act in practice. "VAOM does not replace governance. It operationalizes it."
- The credit risk analogy: risk bands decide which loans are auto-approved, which need an underwriter, which go to committee. Statistical risk is kept separate from institutional authority.
- Eight principles: Controlled Delegation over Blind Automation; Confidence Informs Authority, It Does Not Define It; Architecture Before Acceleration; Compliance as Structural Outcome; Human Accountability Preserved; Versioned Learning Under Change Control; Boundaries Compile to Enforcement ("the most reliable form of non-delegable remains a tool the agent does not have"); Controls Are Proven, Not Presumed ("A control without such evidence is treated as absent").
- Authority bands: Band A, the agent executes; Band B, a human reviews and approves before execution; Band C, escalation to a senior decision-maker or specialist; Non-delegable, the agent may draft or propose but never execute.
- Discovery and design: the decision inventory (decisions hide inside the obvious one), authority decomposition on five dimensions (reversibility, consequence scope, regulatory exposure, confidence measurability, accountability clarity), six delegation patterns (Prepare & Present, Draft & Approve, Triage & Route, Execute & Audit, Monitor & Intervene, Coordinate & Escalate), and six readiness conditions (measurable confidence, explicit authority boundaries, tested escalation, producible audit evidence, assigned accountability, funded and effective oversight).
- The Delegation Authority Matrix: per decision type, the band for each confidence level, value limits, cumulative caps, the accountable role.
- Section 8: confidence thresholds are calibrated per decision type against a declared error target from a labelled sample; the threshold is an output of calibration, not a setting. Value limits derive from expected loss and risk appetite.
- Readiness Condition 6: oversight is funded (review load within funded hours at no more than about 80 percent utilization) and effective. "A queue absorbed by reviewing faster is rubber-stamping by another name." Seeded cases with known errors are disclosed, never execute, and are never used where records feed regulatory reporting, which excludes dismissing AML alerts, whose records feed investigations and regulatory reporting. Reviewer-level measurement is employee monitoring.
- Section 9: the attenuation rule, a sub-agent's authority is always a strict subset of its parent's; boundary verification tests every boundary by attempting to cross it.
- Section 10: continuous assurance and circuit breakers, which only contain.
- Section 11: the Delegation Scorecard, thirteen metrics, judged on evidence.
